scenes.title: What is Git & Version Control?
scenes.narration: Version control records the history of your project so you can track every change, collaborate safely, and travel back in time when needed.

scenes.title: Why Version Control
bullets: It keeps a complete history so you can see who changed what and when.
It lets many people work on the same codebase without overwriting each other.
It gives you a safety net to undo mistakes and return to a known-good state.
scenes.narration: Version control captures a full timeline of your work, answering who changed a line and when they did it. It coordinates teams so several people can edit the same project without stepping on one another. And it acts as a safety net, letting you rewind to any earlier point when something goes wrong.

scenes.title: With vs. Without Git
scenes.narration: Without version control, teams drift into folders full of files named final and final-v2, emailed back and forth and impossible to reconcile. With Git, a single repository holds one authoritative copy plus the entire history of how it evolved. Any team touching code should reach for Git from day one.

scenes.title: Starting a Repository
scenes.code:
git init                 # create a new repo
git status               # see what changed
git add .                # stage all changes
git commit -m "Initial commit"
scenes.narration: You turn any folder into a repository with git init. Running git status shows what has changed since the last save point. The git add command stages the files you want to record, and git commit permanently saves that snapshot with a message describing it.

scenes.text: Git tracks snapshots of your project over time — it is not a backup service, but a complete, navigable history of your work.
scenes.narration: Think of Git as a series of snapshots you can move between at will. It is less about backup and more about a rich, navigable history of everything you have done.
